title: Era 1 Quizzes (Ancient & Classical World) — Batch 2 of 2
subtitle: Questions 1–76 · Authenticated UGC NET Stems, Keys & Explanations

items.title: Quiz Q#251 · Virgil
items.stem: In which work by Virgil does The poet appear as teacher who addresses Maecenas and the farmer?
items.explanation: The poet (The teacher who addresses Maecenas and the farmer) is a central figure in Virgil's Georgics.

items.title: Quiz Q#252 · Virgil
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Toil conquered all things."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Virgil's Georgics (29 BCE).

items.title: Quiz Q#253 · Virgil
items.stem: Which four-book didactic poem in dactylic hexameter by Virgil offers instruction on agriculture, vine-tending, animal husbandry, and beekeeping, concluding with the myth of Aristaeus and Orpheus and Eurydice?
items.explanation: Virgil's Georgics (published c. 29 BCE) is a masterwork of Latin didactic poetry celebrating labor (*labor omnia vicit*) and the restoration of Italy under Octavian.

items.title: Quiz Q#254 · Horace
items.stem: In which work by Horace does Horace appear as speaker, a freedman's son who laughs at folly and at himself?
options: Ars Poetica / Epistle to the Pisones
items.explanation: Horace (The speaker, a freedman's son who laughs at folly and at himself) is a prominent figure in Horace's Satires.

items.title: Quiz Q#255 · Horace
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Speak the truth while laughing."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Horace's Satires (35-30 BCE).

items.title: Quiz Q#256 · Horace
items.stem: Which two-book collection of hexameter conversational poems by Horace (*Sermones*) laughs at human folly with urbane, gentle irony rather than harsh invective, asking 'What prevents one from speaking the truth while laughing?'
options: Ars Poetica / Epistle to the Pisones
items.explanation: Horace's Satires (35–30 BCE) established the genial, witty style of Horatian satire in contrast to the fierce indignation of Lucilius or Juvenal.

items.title: Quiz Q#257 · Horace
items.stem: In which work by Horace does Horace appear as lyric speaker, shifting between private joy and public praise?
options: Ars Poetica / Epistle to the Pisones
items.explanation: Horace (The lyric speaker, shifting between private joy and public praise) is a central figure in Horace's Odes.

items.title: Quiz Q#258 · Horace
items.stem: Which four-book lyric collection by Horace adapts Greek Aeolic meters (Alcaic and Sapphic) into Latin, coining famous phrases such as *carpe diem* ('seize the day') and *dulce et decorum est pro patria mori*?
options: Ars Poetica / Epistle to the Pisones
items.explanation: Horace's Odes (*Carmina*, 23 BCE and 13 BCE) represent the summit of Augustan lyric poetry, celebrated for verbal perfection, philosophical reflection, and civic praise.

items.title: Quiz Q#259 · Horace
items.stem: In which work by Horace does Horace appear as letter writer, a poet turning toward moral questions?
options: Ars Poetica / Epistle to the Pisones
items.explanation: Horace (The letter writer, a poet turning toward moral questions) is a central figure in Horace's Epistles.

items.title: Quiz Q#260 · Horace
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"They change their sky, not their soul."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Horace's Epistles (20-14 BCE).

items.title: Quiz Q#261 · Horace
items.stem: Which collection of letters in dactylic hexameter by Horace, addressed to friends and patrons including Maecenas, explores moral philosophy, the pursuit of wisdom in retirement, and the famous motto *Sapere aude* ('dare to be wise')?
options: Ars Poetica / Epistle to the Pisones
items.explanation: Horace's Epistles (20–14 BCE) reflect his mature philosophical turn toward Stoic and Epicurean ethics, advocating self-mastery and contentment.

items.title: Quiz Q#262 · Horace
items.stem: In which work by Horace does Horace appear as poet giving practical advice in a verse letter?
options: Ars Poetica / Epistle to the Pisones
items.explanation: Horace (The poet giving practical advice in a verse letter) is a central figure in Horace's Ars Poetica / Epistle to the Pisones.

items.title: Quiz Q#263 · Horace
items.stem: Which influential verse epistle by Horace advises aspiring playwrights on decorum, unity of action, beginning *in medias res*, and the dual purpose of poetry to delight and instruct (*aut prodesse volunt aut delectare poetae*)?
options: Ars Poetica / Epistle to the Pisones
items.explanation: Horace's Ars Poetica (c. 19 BCE) served as the primary textbook of classical poetic theory throughout the Renaissance and Neoclassical periods.

items.title: Quiz Q#264 · Lucretius
items.stem: In which work by Lucretius does Lucretius appear as poet teacher who explains Epicurean philosophy?
items.explanation: Lucretius (The poet teacher who explains Epicurean philosophy) is a central figure in Lucretius's De Rerum Natura.

items.title: Quiz Q#265 · Lucretius
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Nothing can be produced from nothing."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Lucretius's De Rerum Natura (by 54 BCE).

items.title: Quiz Q#266 · Lucretius
items.stem: Which six-book philosophical epic in dactylic hexameter by Lucretius expounds Epicurean atomism, arguing that the soul is mortal, the universe consists of atoms and void, and fear of death and the gods should be banished?
items.explanation: Lucretius's De Rerum Natura ('On the Nature of Things', c. 54 BCE) is a monumental philosophical poem designed to liberate humanity from religious superstition through natural philosophy.

items.title: Quiz Q#267 · Catullus
items.stem: In which work by Catullus does Catullus appear as speaker of the personal poems?
items.explanation: Catullus (The speaker of the personal poems) is a central figure in Catullus's Poems / Carmina.

items.title: Quiz Q#268 · Catullus
items.stem: Which collection of 116 lyric, elegiac, and epigrammatic poems by Catullus vividly chronicles his tumultuous love affair with 'Lesbia' (Clodia Metelli), containing the famous paradox *Odi et amo* ('I hate and I love')?
items.explanation: Catullus's Carmina (c. 84–54 BCE) pioneered Latin personal lyric poetry, blending intense emotional intimacy with exquisite Alexandrian craft.

items.title: Quiz Q#269 · Ovid
items.stem: In which work by Ovid does Daphne appear as A nymph who becomes a laurel tree to escape Apollo?
items.explanation: Daphne (A nymph who becomes a laurel tree to escape Apollo) is a central figure in Ovid's Metamorphoses.

items.title: Quiz Q#270 · Ovid
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Bodies changed into new forms."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ovid's Metamorphoses (c. 8 CE).

items.title: Quiz Q#271 · Ovid
items.stem: Which epic in fifteen books by Ovid weaves together over 250 mythological tales of physical transformation from the creation of the world down to the deification of Julius Caesar?
items.explanation: Ovid's Metamorphoses (completed c. 8 CE) is the greatest mythographic poem of antiquity, exerting an immense influence on European literature from Chaucer and Shakespeare to modern times.

items.title: Quiz Q#272 · Ovid
items.stem: In which work by Ovid does Penelope appear as Odysseus' wife, writing while she waits at home?
items.explanation: Penelope (Odysseus' wife, writing while she waits at home) is a prominent figure in Ovid's Heroides.

items.title: Quiz Q#273 · Ovid
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The result justifies the means."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ovid's Heroides (c. 15 BCE).

items.title: Quiz Q#274 · Ovid
items.stem: Which innovative collection of fifteen fictional verse letters by Ovid is written in elegiac couplets from the perspective of legendary heroines (such as Penelope, Dido, and Ariadne) lamenting their absent or faithless lovers?
items.explanation: Ovid's Heroides (c. 15 BCE) founded the epistolary genre in European literature, showcasing intense psychological exploration of female abandonment and longing.

items.title: Quiz Q#275 · Ovid
items.stem: In which work by Ovid does The lover appear as Ovid's playful speaker, not a plain record of his life?
items.explanation: The lover (Ovid's playful speaker, not a plain record of his life) is a prominent figure in Ovid's Amores.

items.title: Quiz Q#276 · Ovid
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Every lover is a soldier."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ovid's Amores (c. 16 BCE).

items.title: Quiz Q#277 · Ovid
items.stem: Which collection of elegiac love poems in three books by Ovid playfully chronicles his romantic adventures in Rome with an elusive mistress named Corinna?
items.explanation: Ovid's Amores (c. 16 BCE) is a witty, lighthearted masterpiece of Latin erotic elegy depicting love as a military campaign (*militat omnis amans*).

items.title: Quiz Q#278 · Ovid
items.stem: In which work by Ovid does The teacher of love appear as Ovid's speaker, who claims to teach seduction?
items.explanation: The teacher of love (Ovid's speaker, who claims to teach seduction) is a prominent figure in Ovid's Ars Amatoria.

items.title: Quiz Q#279 · Ovid
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Ovid was our teacher."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Ovid's Ars Amatoria (c. 2 BCE).

items.title: Quiz Q#280 · Ovid
items.stem: Which didactic mock-treatise in elegiac couplets by Ovid offers humorous, worldly instruction to men and women on how to find, seduce, and keep a lover, scandalizing conservative Roman morals?
items.explanation: Ovid's Ars Amatoria ('The Art of Love', c. 2 BCE) is believed to have contributed to Emperor Augustus's decision to banish Ovid to Tomis in 8 CE on the pretext of *carmen et error* ('a poem and a mistake').

items.title: Quiz Q#281 · Seneca
items.stem: In which work by Seneca does Agamemnon appear as king of Argos, killed after his victory at Troy?
items.explanation: Agamemnon (The king of Argos, killed after his victory at Troy) is a central figure in Seneca's Agamemnon.

items.title: Quiz Q#282 · Seneca
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The ghost of Thyestes demands revenge."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Seneca's Agamemnon (1st century CE).

items.title: Quiz Q#283 · Seneca
items.stem: Which closet drama by Seneca depicts the ghost of Thyestes prophesying vengeance on Agamemnon, culminating in the king's brutal assassination by Clytemnestra and Aegisthus upon his return from Troy?
items.explanation: Seneca's Agamemnon (1st century CE) is a grim Roman tragedy marked by stoic fatalism, dark rhetoric, and bloody horrors that influenced Elizabethan revenge tragedy.

items.title: Quiz Q#284 · Seneca
items.stem: In which work by Seneca does Medea appear as A princess and witch who speaks more than half the play?
items.explanation: Medea (A princess and witch who speaks more than half the play) is a central figure in Seneca's Medea.

items.title: Quiz Q#285 · Seneca
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"There are no gods in heaven."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Seneca's Medea (1st century CE).

items.title: Quiz Q#286 · Seneca
items.stem: In which bloody Roman tragedy by Seneca does the Colchian sorceress summon underworld furies, slaughter her two children on stage in front of Jason, and fly off in a dragon-drawn chariot?
items.explanation: Seneca's Medea (1st century CE) portrays uncontrolled passion (*furor*) overpowering rational restraint (*mens*), creating an archetype of the demonic avenger.

items.title: Quiz Q#287 · Seneca
items.stem: In which work by Seneca does Oedipus appear as King of Thebes, who learns the truth of his birth and his crime?
items.explanation: Oedipus (King of Thebes, who learns the truth of his birth and his crime) is a central figure in Seneca's Oedipus.

items.title: Quiz Q#288 · Seneca
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The crimes that I have fled from."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Seneca's Oedipus (1st century CE).

items.title: Quiz Q#289 · Seneca
items.stem: Which tragedy by Seneca emphasizes dark necromancy, liver divination, and macabre horror as Oedipus tears out his own eyes and Jocasta commits suicide on stage with a sword thrust into her womb?
items.explanation: Seneca's Oedipus (1st century CE) recasts the Sophoclean myth with intense baroque sensationalism and fatalistic despair.

items.title: Quiz Q#290 · Seneca
items.stem: In which work by Seneca does Phaedra appear as Wife of Theseus, who openly pursues her stepson?
items.explanation: Phaedra (Wife of Theseus, who openly pursues her stepson) is a central figure in Seneca's Phaedra.

items.title: Quiz Q#291 · Seneca
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"I stirred my stepmother to love."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Seneca's Phaedra (1st century CE).

items.title: Quiz Q#292 · Seneca
items.stem: In which Senecan tragedy does Phaedra passionately confess her incestuous lust directly to Hippolytus, falsely accuse him with his left-behind sword, and later commit suicide over his mutilated corpse?
items.explanation: Seneca's Phaedra (1st century CE) emphasizes the destructive power of *furor* and served as a direct model for Racine's Phèdre.

items.title: Quiz Q#293 · Seneca
items.stem: In which work by Seneca does Atreus appear as King who plans a cannibal feast as revenge?
items.explanation: Atreus (King who plans a cannibal feast as revenge) is a central figure in Seneca's Thyestes.

items.title: Quiz Q#294 · Seneca
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"I recognize my brother."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Seneca's Thyestes (1st century CE).

items.title: Quiz Q#295 · Seneca
items.stem: Which Senecan revenge tragedy features King Atreus serving his brother Thyestes a banquet containing the butchered, roasted flesh of Thyestes's own sons?
items.explanation: Seneca's Thyestes (1st century CE) is the most horrifying of Senecan plays, directly inspiring the cannibalistic banquet in Shakespeare's Titus Andronicus.

items.title: Quiz Q#296 · Juvenal
items.stem: In which work by Juvenal does The satiric speaker appear as An angry voice that attacks Rome's vices?
items.explanation: The satiric speaker (An angry voice that attacks Rome's vices) is a prominent figure in Juvenal's Satires.

items.title: Quiz Q#297 · Juvenal
items.stem: Which collection of sixteen hexameter poems in five books attacks the moral decadence, hypocrisy, and foreigners of imperial Rome with biting indignation (*facit indignatio versum*), coining 'panem et circenses' ('bread and circuses')?
items.explanation: Juvenal's Satires (early 2nd century CE) created the bitter, searing mode of Juvenalian satire that deeply influenced Samuel Johnson's London and The Vanity of Human Wishes.

items.title: Quiz Q#298 · Martial
items.stem: In which work by Martial does Martial appear as poet speaker, often a client asking patrons for notice or gifts?
items.explanation: Martial (The poet speaker, often a client asking patrons for notice or gifts) is a central figure in Martial's Epigrams.

items.title: Quiz Q#299 · Martial
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"I live in a little cell."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Martial's Epigrams (c. 86–102 CE; books published over time).

items.title: Quiz Q#300 · Martial
items.stem: Which collection of over 1,500 short, witty poems in twelve books by Martial realistically captures the daily gossip, vices, and spectacles of Flavian Rome, perfecting the stinging sting-in-the-tail ending?
items.explanation: Martial's Epigrams (c. 86–103 CE) established the classical epigram as a concise, biting poetic form culminating in an unexpected punchline.

items.title: Quiz Q#301 · Plutarch
items.stem: In which work by Plutarch does Plutarch appear as biographer who compares each Greek and Roman pair?
items.explanation: Plutarch (The biographer who compares each Greek and Roman pair) is a central figure in Plutarch's Parallel Lives.

items.title: Quiz Q#302 · Plutarch
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Not histories, but lives."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Plutarch's Parallel Lives (c. 100–120 CE; individual lives vary).

items.title: Quiz Q#303 · Plutarch
items.stem: Which biographical masterpiece pairs famous Greek and Roman statesmen and generals (such as Alexander and Caesar, Demosthenes and Cicero) followed by a formal moral comparison (*synkrisis*)?
items.explanation: Plutarch's Parallel Lives (c. 100–120 CE), translated into English by Sir Thomas North in 1579, served as the primary source for Shakespeare's Roman plays (Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra, Coriolanus).

items.title: Quiz Q#304 · Plutarch
items.stem: In which work by Plutarch does Plutarch appear as essayist and usual speaker of the moral pieces?
items.explanation: Plutarch (The essayist and usual speaker of the moral pieces) is a central figure in Plutarch's Moralia.

items.title: Quiz Q#305 · Plutarch
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Painting is silent poetry."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Plutarch's Moralia (1st–2nd century CE; collection assembled over tim).

items.title: Quiz Q#306 · Plutarch
items.stem: Which encyclopedic collection of seventy-eight essays and dialogues by Plutarch covers ethics, literary criticism, religion, science, and the famous essay 'On the Education of Children'?
items.explanation: Plutarch's Moralia (early 2nd century CE) exerted a profound influence on European essayists, particularly Michel de Montaigne.

items.title: Quiz Q#307 · Quintilian
items.stem: In which work by Quintilian does Quintilian appear as teacher speaking as the author of the whole course?
items.explanation: Quintilian (The teacher speaking as the author of the whole course) is a central figure in Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria.

items.title: Quiz Q#308 · Quintilian
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The good man skilled at speaking."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria (c. 95 CE).

items.title: Quiz Q#309 · Quintilian
items.stem: Which twelve-book pedagogical treatise by Quintilian outlines the complete education of the orator from infancy to retirement, defining the ideal speaker as 'a good man skilled in speaking' (*vir bonus dicendi peritus*)?
items.explanation: Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria ('Institutes of Oratory', c. 95 CE) was the authoritative educational manual of the Renaissance, championing moral integrity alongside rhetorical eloquence.

items.title: Quiz Q#310 · Longinus
items.stem: In which work by Longinus does Longinus appear as unknown author, often called Pseudo-Longinus?
items.explanation: Longinus (The unknown author, often called Pseudo-Longinus) is a central figure in Longinus's On the Sublime.

items.title: Quiz Q#311 · Longinus
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Sublimity is the echo of a great soul."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Longinus's On the Sublime (1554).

items.title: Quiz Q#312 · Longinus
items.stem: Which foundational treatise on literary criticism (*Peri Hypsous*) analyzes five sources of grandeur in writing, defining the 'sublime' as an echo of a great soul (*megalophrosynes apechema*) that transports the audience with ecstasy?
items.explanation: Longinus's On the Sublime (1st century CE) shifted literary criticism from mechanical rule-following to the emotional elevation and imaginative transport of art.

items.title: Quiz Q#313 · Tertullian
items.stem: In which work by Tertullian does Tertullian appear as speaker, a Christian advocate addressing Roman officials?
items.explanation: Tertullian (The speaker, a Christian advocate addressing Roman officials) is a central figure in Tertullian's Christian apologetic works.

items.title: Quiz Q#314 · Tertullian
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"The blood of Christians is seed."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Tertullian's Christian apologetic works (c. 197–220 CE; individual works vary).

items.title: Quiz Q#315 · Tertullian
items.stem: Which North African Church Father famously challenged pagan philosophy by asking 'What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord is there between the Academy and the Church?' in his defense of Christian faith?
items.explanation: Tertullian (c. 155–220 CE), writing in vigorous Latin in Carthage, produced landmark apologetic works including the Apologeticus defending Christians against Roman persecution.

items.title: Quiz Q#316 · St. Augustine
items.stem: In which work by St. Augustine does Augustine appear as speaker, who tells his sins and his conversion as a prayer?
items.explanation: Augustine (The speaker, who tells his sins and his conversion as a prayer) is a central figure in St. Augustine's Confessions.

items.title: Quiz Q#317 · St. Augustine
items.stem: Which spiritual autobiography in thirteen books by St. Augustine traces his conversion from sinful youth and Manichaeism to Christian baptism, famously recounting the theft of pears and the voice chanting 'Tolle, lege' ('Pick up and read')?
items.explanation: St. Augustine's Confessions (c. 397–400 CE) inaugurated psychological self-examination and autobiography in Western literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#318 · St. Augustine
items.stem: In which work by St. Augustine does Augustine appear as author, who argues against pagan blame of Christianity?
items.explanation: Augustine (The author, who argues against pagan blame of Christianity) is a central figure in St. Augustine's The City of God.

items.title: Quiz Q#319 · St. Augustine
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Two loves have made two cities."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in St. Augustine's The City of God (426).

items.title: Quiz Q#320 · St. Augustine
items.stem: Which monumental twenty-two-book theological and historical work was written by St. Augustine in response to the pagan accusation that the sack of Rome in 410 CE was caused by the abandonment of the traditional gods?
items.explanation: St. Augustine's De Civitate Dei ('The City of God', 413–426 CE) articulates a Christian philosophy of history contrasting the Earthly City driven by self-love with the City of God driven by love of God.

items.title: Quiz Q#321 · Jerome
items.stem: In which work by Jerome does Jerome appear as scholar who revised and translated the Latin biblical text?
items.explanation: Jerome (The scholar who revised and translated the Latin biblical text) is a central figure in Jerome's Latin Vulgate Bible — translation/revision.

items.title: Quiz Q#322 · Jerome
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"It is necessary to seek the single fountainhead."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Jerome's Latin Vulgate Bible — translation/revision (405).

items.title: Quiz Q#323 · Jerome
items.stem: Which monumental translation of the Hebrew and Greek Scriptures into idiomatic Latin, commissioned by Pope Damasus I in 382 CE, became the official Bible of the Western Church for over a millennium?
items.explanation: St. Jerome's Vulgate Bible (completed c. 405 CE in Bethlehem) established the linguistic standard of medieval Christendom and theological scholarship.

items.title: Quiz Q#324 · Boethius
items.stem: In which work by Boethius does Boethius appear as prisoner who complains and then learns?
items.explanation: Boethius (The prisoner who complains and then learns) is a central figure in Boethius's The Consolation of Philosophy.

items.title: Quiz Q#325 · Boethius
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following line?
"Nothing is miserable unless you think it so."
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Boethius's The Consolation of Philosophy (524).

items.title: Quiz Q#326 · Boethius
items.stem: Which philosophical dialogue in prosimetrum (alternating prose and verse) was written in prison while the author awaited execution under King Theodoric, featuring Lady Philosophy explaining the Wheel of Fortune and divine providence?
items.explanation: Boethius's De Consolatione Philosophiae (524 CE) was one of the most widely read and translated works of the Middle Ages, translated by King Alfred, Chaucer, and Queen Elizabeth I.
